offence_severity: Life imprisonment / Rigorous imprisonment for five years
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution failed to recover the weapon of crime, obtain a ballistic opinion, and examine a ballistic expert, which significantly weakened the prosecution's case.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses' evidence as suffering from serious lacunae and could not be said to be credible.
trial_duration: Trial judgment: 05.02.2018; High Court decision: 05.02.2018; Supreme Court decision: 21 February 2024
legal_representation: Pradeep Kumar Mathur, Chiranjeev Johri, Chandra Nand Jha, M.K. Tiwari, Sitesh Kumar, Arvind Kumar, Advs. for the Appellant; Rana Mukherjee, Sr. Adv., Samarth Mohanty, Ankit Goel, Advs. for the Respondent
procedural_irregularity: Non-recovery of the weapon of crime, non-examination of ballistic expert, non-obtaining of ballistic opinion
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence imposed; High Court: Conviction and sentence confirmed; Supreme Court: Conviction and sentence set aside
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant Ram Singh was responsible for the death of the deceased, Dulli, by firing a shot from a country made pistol at her. They relied on the testimony of PW-1, the son of the deceased, and other witnesses, including the police investigation and post-mortem report. The prosecution claimed that the evidence, including the eyewitness accounts, was sufficient to prove the appellant's guilt beyond all reasonable doubt.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution's case was flawed due to glaring inconsistencies in the eyewitness accounts, the non-recovery of the weapon of crime, and the failure to obtain a ballistic report or examine a ballistic expert. They contended that the evidence was not credible and that the trial court and High Court erred in convicting the appellant while acquitting the co-accused Lala Ram on the same set of evidence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that non-recovery of the weapon of crime and non-examination of a ballistic expert do not automatically invalidate the prosecution's case, but if the evidence suffers from glaring inconsistencies and material witnesses are not examined, the omission may be fatal to the prosecution's case. The court also emphasized the principle of parity, stating that similar evidence against two accused cannot result in one being convicted and the other acquitted.
precedent_relied_upon: Javed Shaukat Ali Qureshi Vs. State of Gujarat, [2023] 12 SCR 220 : (2023) 9 SCC 164; Munna Lal Vs. State of U.P., [2023] 3 SCR 224 : (2023) SCC Online SC 80; Gurucharan Singh Vs. State of Punjab, [1963] 3 SCR 585 : AIR 1963 SC 340; Sukhwant Singh Vs. State of Punjab, [1995] 2 SCR 1190 : (1995) 3 SCC 367; State of Punjab Vs. Jugraj Singh, [2002] 1 SCR 998 : (2002) 3 SCC 234; Gulab Vs. State of U.P., [2021] 9 SCR 678 : (2022) 12 SCC 677; Pritinder Singh Vs. State of Punjab, [2023] 10 SCR 1033 : (2023) 7 SCC 727
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution failed to prove the appellant's guilt beyond all reasonable doubt. The Supreme Court found the evidence to be inconsistent and not credible, and the non-recovery of the weapon, non-examination of the ballistic expert, and failure to examine material witnesses rendered the prosecution's case insufficient to justify conviction.
